source.title: Block Transformer: Global-to-Local Language Modeling for Fast Inference
source.authors: Sangmin Bae; Adam Fisch; Namgyu Ho; Hyunjik Jo; Taehyeon Kim; Yireun Kim; Tal Schuster; James Thorne; SeYoung Yun

record.tranche_reason: The study compares architectural variants at fixed parameter counts and reports their language-modeling losses, bearing on whether architecture details make little difference.
record.gate_note: The study does not fit or assess power laws, extrapolate scaling curves, or find compute-optimal parameter/token allocations. Its reported loss and downstream-task results across model sizes are not tests of predictive scaling relationships. The rows below cover architecture ablations that bear on V4; some plotted values are not numerically available in the text.
record.test_reason: This is an architecture paper on inference throughput, so it does not test the claim. It cites Kaplan and Hoffmann only to frame its IsoFLOP section and fits no power laws, extrapolations or compute-optimal splits. The allocation-ratio, block-length, embedder and token-decoder ablations compare components of a new hierarchical model, not depth and width of a standard transformer. Changing the block-to-token allocation at fixed parameters also changes FLOPs per token, since the block decoder runs once per LB tokens, so these are not shape-at-fixed-size tests. Loss magnitudes are figure-only.
record.authors_conclusion: Partly right. The authors conclude that both the global block decoder and the local token decoder are vital, and that a balanced (1:1) allocation beats the decoder-heavy splits favoured by MEGABYTE. Block Transformers reach 10–20x inference throughput over vanilla transformers of equal perplexity, at the cost of more parameters and FLOPs.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains a hierarchical global-to-local architecture and compares its architectural ablations; it does not reproduce a scaling-law fitting procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: Loss varies with decoder parameter-allocation ratio, block length, embedder design, token-decoder design, and prefix length.

fits_no_version.finding: In the hierarchical Block Transformer at fixed non-embedding parameters, loss is U-shaped across block:token decoder allocation, with 1:1 optimal at LB=4. The optimum shifts with block length, and component choices (CLS embedder, cross-attention decoder) worsen loss.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In global-to-local hierarchical transformers, the parameter split between global and local modules materially affects loss at fixed parameter count.

fits_no_version.finding: At equal non-embedding parameters, Block Transformers have higher loss than vanilla models (e.g. 85M: 2.753 vs 2.476, Table 1). They need about 2–3x the parameters to match.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Architecture class (hierarchical vs vanilla attention), not shape, shifts loss at fixed parameter count.

record.problems: The ablation results relevant to V4 are mainly presented in figures without numeric loss values or uncertainty estimates. Some reported comparisons vary architecture components rather than standard depth and width.
record.rows_left_out: No rows were included for the model-size loss table, downstream-task scores, throughput measurements, IsoFLOP analysis, or long-context evaluations because they do not test the versions of the scaling-law claim identified as tested here.

untested.parts: No power-law fit of loss in parameters, tokens or compute. Table 1 lists losses by size only.
The IsoFLOP analysis imposes a throughput constraint and does not estimate a loss-optimal N/D split versus compute.
No depth/width/aspect-ratio sweep of a standard transformer at fixed parameters.
Text pretraining only. Uptraining is reported as recovery, not as a power law.
Zero-shot scores are reported but not modelled against scale or loss.
No exponents or fitting choices compared.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'challenges' and 'limits_scope' labels on V4 are dropped. The ablations vary components and allocation inside a novel hierarchical architecture, with FLOPs per token not held fixed, and give no numeric losses. Settings for Sec 3.4 conflict: the Fig 3 caption says 8B tokens with lookup and prefix length 2, while G.5 says 26B tokens with a CLS default.

versions.untested_parts: No power-law fits or tests over parameters, training tokens, or compute; model-size comparisons alone do not assess the claimed functional form.
No small-run fits are used to predict larger-run losses.
The IsoFLOP experiment constrains training FLOPs and inference throughput; it does not test the loss-minimizing parameter/token split as a function of compute.
The study tests allocation ratios, block lengths, and selected component designs, not a broad sweep of depth and width.
Only text language modeling is studied; other modalities and training regimes are not tested.
Downstream benchmarks are reported, but the study does not test their predictability from scale or pretraining loss.
No scaling-law exponents or compute-optimal split are fitted or compared across fitting choices.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.reason: At fixed total non-embedding parameters, the paper reports a clear U-shaped loss trade-off across decoder allocations, with noticeable declines when either decoder is too small; block length also shifts the preferred allocation (R1-R6).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Reported loss differs by component choice: the CLS-token and cross-attention options compromise performance, while longer prefixes improve it (R7-R12).
